summary: A serpent challenges the garden command, and the woman and man eat the forbidden fruit, become aware of their nakedness, and hide. God questions them, announces painful consequences for serpent, woman, and man, clothes the pair, and sends them from the garden with the way to the tree of life guarded.
whyItMatters: The rupture of trust, blame, toil, and exile alters the relationships introduced in chapters 1–2. The chapter leaves the question of life outside Eden for the next generations.

context.author: Genesis names no historical writer. Jewish and Christian tradition associates the Torah with Moses; the book briefing describes older traditions shaped into a final literary form, without a settled account of every stage.
context.audience: The book addresses Israel through a story of shared human origins and the family from whom Israel traces its ancestry; no single first audience is named in this chapter.
context.date: The narrated events belong to primeval or ancestral time, not to a securely dated writing event. Major stages of Genesis are often placed across the monarchic to Persian periods, with exact models and dates debated.
context.setting: The garden of Eden and the ground outside it after expulsion.
context.literaryForm: Garden temptation and interrogation narrative followed by divine speeches and an expulsion scene.

before.text: The man and woman have a garden, a broad food permission with one boundary, and an unashamed relationship. The serpent now asks about that specific command.

here.text: Watch the difference between God’s command, the serpent’s claims, the pair’s action, and the distinct consequences spoken to each.

after.text: Outside the garden, the next chapter begins with Cain and Abel and shows violence entering the first family.

outline.heading: Serpent disputes the command
outline.note: The dialogue reframes the food prohibition and promises knowledge.

outline.heading: Eating, exposure, and hiding
outline.note: Both eat, cover themselves, and hide from God.

outline.heading: Questions and blame
outline.note: God addresses the man and woman, who each identify another participant.

outline.heading: Consequences for serpent, woman, and man
outline.note: The speeches describe hostility, painful childbirth, domination, arduous work, and death.

outline.heading: Clothing and exclusion from the tree of life
outline.note: The man names Eve, God clothes them, and guards the garden entrance.

keyVerses.text: When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate. Then she gave some to her husband with her, and he ate it, too.
keyVerses.why: Both members of the pair eat, turning the garden prohibition into action.

keyVerses.text: To the woman he said, “I will greatly multiply your pain in childbirth. You will bear children in pain. Your desire will be for your husband, and he will rule over you.”
keyVerses.why: The speech to the woman names pain and rule, a difficult consequence that should be read as such.

keyVerses.text: So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.
keyVerses.why: The guarded way to the tree of life makes expulsion the chapter’s final condition.

questions.question: Who is the serpent in this chapter?
questions.answer: The opening calls it a subtle animal of the field made by God. Later traditions identify the serpent with other evil figures, but this chapter itself does not name Satan or explain an unseen biography.

questions.question: How does the serpent change the food command?
questions.answer: It asks whether God forbade every tree, even though the prior command allowed every tree except one. The woman replies with the restriction and adds not touching; the serpent then denies the threatened death.

questions.question: Is the woman alone responsible for the eating?
questions.answer: No. The woman takes and eats, gives fruit to her husband with her, and he eats. God questions both, and the speech to the man explicitly addresses his own eating of the forbidden fruit.

questions.question: Why do they hide after their eyes are opened?
questions.answer: They recognize their nakedness, sew coverings, and fear God’s presence. The change contrasts with the previous chapter’s unashamed nakedness, while the story lets the man explain his own fear.

questions.question: Does “he will rule over you” command men to dominate women?
questions.answer: The line occurs among the painful consequences spoken after disobedience, alongside multiplied childbirth pain. It describes a damaged relationship in the story; the chapter does not present domination as the earlier ideal or instruct readers to impose it.

questions.question: What exactly is promised in the hostility between serpent and offspring?
questions.answer: God announces continuing hostility and a blow to head and heel. The verse does not identify a named future individual or spell out a later redemption scheme, even though later readers have connected it to one.

questions.question: What are cherubim doing at the end?
questions.answer: They are stationed east of the garden with a turning flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. The chapter uses them as guardians in this scene without explaining their origin or complete nature.

questions.question: Why does God bar access to the tree of life?
questions.answer: The stated concern is that the human might take from it and live forever after gaining knowledge of good and evil. Expulsion and the guarded entrance carry out that concern; the text does not describe this as an invitation to return immediately.

glossary.def: The serpent’s shrewd quality in the opening description, shown in its questioning of the command.
The beings stationed to guard the path to the tree of life after expulsion.
Unwanted plants named among the growth that will make working the ground difficult.
